value: Epictetus: people are disturbed not by things but by the view they take of them
runnerUp: A, if the central idea is read as simply the bird's right to sing its song
reasoning: The speaker first blames the bird for singing, then admits 'The fault must partly have been in me.' The trouble was his own attitude, not the bird. Epictetus says exactly this: we are disturbed by the view we take of things, not by the things themselves.
In the first stanza the speaker wishes the bird would fly away and claps his hands at it because he 'could bear no more'. That is annoyance, that is, irritation.

The pattern 'enough of ... to know' shows a sufficient amount: 'I have seen enough of his work to know that he is ready.' 'Few', 'a few' and 'several' do not fit with 'his work' and the 'to know' that follows.
'People' is countable, so we use 'few' (not 'little' or 'much'): 'only few make the grade' means a very small number succeed.
In reported speech 'me' becomes 'him' and 'now' becomes 'then', and a request is reported with 'to': 'The boy requested them to let him work then.'
'Some of these facts' refers to more than one fact, so the plural verb 'are' is used.
A negative command is reported with 'not to', and 'your' changes to 'their' for the boys: 'She told the boys not to waste their money.'
'At this time tomorrow' describes an action in progress at a future moment, so the future continuous tense is used: 'we shall be presenting'.
'Each' is singular, so it takes the singular verb: 'Each of the suspected men was arrested.'
The subject is 'only one', which is singular, and 'not done' needs the present perfect helper: 'Only one of the boys has not done the homework.'
An imperative sentence gives a command or request. 'Open the windows.' is a command. A is a wish (optative), and B and D are statements.
